summary: Follow-up on last week's POC reliability incident. Team reviewed 5xx/timeouts patterns, traced to retry/backoff interactions under bursty traffic and an uncovered edge case in prefix caching on a particular model variant. Action items: share logs, run controlled load test, consider short-term Dedicated burst, tune retry/backoff, and schedule postmortem.
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-04-23 16:00 UTC | Duration: 45m | Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Marta Ruiz (Redwood CSM), Carlos Mendes (CTO - Nimbus), Aisha Tan (SRE), Leo Park (ML Eng), Sophie Duval (Product)

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll kick off. Quick agenda: recap last week's incident, what we learned from the logs, immediate mitigations, and next steps. Priya, you want to start with the findings?

[00:18] Priya: Yeah sure. So we pulled the traces overnight, and big picture, the 5xx spikes lined up with a period of sudden traffic burst from your staging harness, right between 11:12 and 11:18. We saw a pattern where requests hit a particular model variant that had lower context cache hit rates — the K V cache, prefix cache, whatever your telemetry calls it, uh, had higher misses so latency spiked which interacted poorly with client-side retries.

[00:42] Aisha: Right, I can confirm, that was when we ramped the scenario to simulate production load. We did notice a bunch of 504/timeouts reported from our side and then we chased with retries which led to more concurrency.

[00:55] Leo: I think one of the things — just to add — the client SDK default retry backoff is pretty aggressive, and we were using that out of the box. We may need to tune that for your hosted environment.

[01:12] Priya: Exactly. So the root is twofold: service-side elevated tail latency (some long tail requests hitting slower kernel path on that quantized variant) plus retry storms from the client. When the latency goes up the retries pile on and we observe 5xx because internal request queues exceed thresholds and start returning 503.

[01:35] Carlos: Quick question — is this specific to the model we're using for the POC or general across Redwood? Could switching to a different variant or moving to a dedicated pool avoid it?

[01:47] Priya: Good question. It's mostly tied to that model variant and the quantization profile we used for the POC. If you switch to a variant with a higher cache locality or lower optimistic quantization the tail improves. Dedicated capacity gives you headroom too — fewer multi-tenant interference spikes and predictable throughput. But it doesn't magically fix client retry behavior.

[02:08] Jordan: Also worth noting, the Dedicated burst option we discussed can reduce queuing by reserving GPU slots for you during peak. We'll send numbers.

[02:20] Sophie: Are there any quick mitigations we can implement on our side today to reduce 5xx while we wait for logs?

[02:27] Priya: On the client: increase base backoff and add jitter, reduce max retries, and add a 429-aware backoff if you get rate limits. On the server side we've temporarily increased request queue length for your pool and tightened rate limiting to soften bursts — that helped in our canary this morning.

[02:48] Aisha: You said you tightened rate limits — do we have visibility into those events? We want to see exact timestamps so we can correlate with our traces.

[02:56] Priya: Yes, we will share filtered logs with redactions. There will be request ids and timestamps. We'll also include the internal error codes; sometimes the transcript of the error looks like 'executor oom' but it's actually a queued timeout.

[03:12] Leo: One thing I noticed in our logs, some client requests were re-sent with slightly different payloads — possible duplicate side effects for downstream services. We need to make sure idempotency keys are in place.

[03:24] Jordan: Good call. We'll recommend idempotency headers in the SDK docs; I'll add that to the follow up.

[03:30] Marta: Quick housekeeping: I'll drop the incident tracker link in the calendar invite after this call so everyone's got the board.

[03:37] Carlos: Ok let's dig into the traces that Priya mentioned. Priya, can you walk us through a representative 5xx trace from 11:14?

[03:45] Priya: Sure. Pulling it up now — so at t=0 we see a request arriving, it's a longer sequence length than typical, so the KV/prefix cache miss causes a cold path. Processing time jumps from 120 ms to 1.2s for that request. Meanwhile the client retries after 300ms, another request queues, the executor sees transient pressure and responds 503. The client then retries again, compounding the problem. The sequence: long tail -> retry -> queue saturation -> 503/504.

[04:25] Aisha: Is there a way to detect that pattern automatically? Like alert if retry rate spikes or if queue depth goes above threshold?

[04:32] Priya: Yes, in the console we can create alerts on token-per-second and 5xx rate as well as queue depth. We can also instrument a retry metric from our SDK if you roll that out.

[04:45] Jordan: For the short term we propose three things: (1) you tune client retries (we'll provide recommended settings), (2) run a controlled load test with the same payloads to reproduce and collect traces, (3) we share logs + consider a Dedicated burst while you ramp. Does that sound reasonable?

[05:00] Carlos: Yes. On the dedicated burst — how fast can that be provisioned and what's the cost implication?

[05:06] Jordan: We can provision a short-term Dedicated slice within 24 hours in most cases; cost estimate I'll send by EOD, it's pro-rated for the time used. For longer term we can discuss Reserved Dedicated capacity.

[05:18] Leo: Any changes needed code-wise for model variant swap? We don't want functional regressions.

[05:23] Priya: Swapping variant is just a model id change in the request; but you should run a small quality check. We can help with eval prompts; small differences in tokenization or generation can appear with different quantization.

[05:40] Sophie: Could the issue be related to our unusually long context inputs? We're sending combined user history and product metadata, sometimes 3k tokens.

[05:48] Priya: Long context increases compute and kernel path selection — if most requests are shorter it's fine, but a mix of short and long causes resource skew. One mitigation is prefix trimming or caching early tokens. Redwood has prefix caching but it depends on hit rates. If you can canonicalize or compress the prompt we can improve hit rates.

[06:12] Carlos: I want to understand what the 'queue length' number means in the console — is that per GPU, per pod, per customer?

[06:20] Priya: It's per serving instance/pod. For Dedicated it's much more predictable because instances are reserved for you. For hosted it's shared and subject to multi-tenant scheduling.

[06:33] Aisha: We also saw a few 502s with 'timeout while streaming' — those seem separate from the 503s. Any idea?

[06:40] Priya: Streaming timeouts often come from long-lived streams hitting idle timeouts or intermittent network blips. We'll check network logs, but initial hunch is the same root cause: long tail processing causing the stream to fall behind and hit the streaming timeout threshold.

[06:58] Jordan: Ok, pragmatically, Priya will share the redacted logs and a one-page write-up of the probable root cause. Aisha's team will run the Friday load test using the script Leo will produce, and Jordan will send Dedicated burst pricing. Marta will set the postmortem invite.

[07:15] Priya: Also want to mention we rolled out a temporary per-customer rate limit tweak for Nimbus during the incident window; it helped stabilize. We'll annotate those events in the logs we send.

[07:28] Sophie: Sounds good. One more question — about security/compliance, will sharing logs expose PII? We need assurance they'll be redacted.

[07:36] Priya: Yes, logs will be sanitized. We'll remove request text and PII; you get IDs/timestamps and internal error codes. If you prefer a handoff session where we walk through logs together we can do that as well.

[07:49] Carlos: Let's do a joint debugging session — maybe Monday.

[07:53] Jordan: Monday works. I'll propose two slots.

[08:00] Aisha: Quick nit — our observability folks want to ingest some Redwood metrics directly into our monitoring stack. Is that available?

[08:07] Priya: We have a metrics export route and we can push a prometheus scrape endpoint for Dedicated customers or a push gateway for hosted. We'll follow up with details.

[08:20] Leo: Regarding SDK versions — which SDK are you recommending? We were on 1.2.0 but saw a note about backoff improvements in 1.3.

[08:27] Jordan: We recommend latest 1.3.x which includes improved jitter/backoff and idempotency helpers. We'll link the changelog.

[08:38] Sophie: Anything else on the timeline for fixes?

[08:42] Priya: Short term: recommended SDK changes + run controlled test (1-2 days). Medium: swap model variant or repin to a less-aggressive quantization (2-5 days). Dedicated provisioning: ~24 hours after signature for a short burst. Postmortem meeting Monday to lock down RCA and next steps.

[08:58] Carlos: Ok good. Let's move to wrap-up and next steps.

[09:03] Jordan: Recap: Priya share logs and write-up; Aisha run load test, Leo provide script; Jordan send Dedicated cost; Marta schedule postmortem; everyone review and come with any further artifacts.

[09:18] Aisha: One last thing, do you have recommendations for idempotency header standard? We use X-Idempotency-Key — is that enough?

[09:25] Priya: That's fine. Use a stable unique key per user action; server will respect it for non-idempotent ops. We'll add an example in the SDK guide.

[09:35] Jordan: Great, thanks all. We'll follow up in email with links to the log share, the rate-limit annotations, and the Dedicated pricing.

[09:44] (call ends)

Notes: transcript contains occasional transcription artifacts (e.g., 'K V cache' vs 'KV cache', 'redwood dedi' shorthand). Several cross-talk moments and filler words present.
